title: TCS commits $7.4B to a one-gigawatt AI campus in Hyderabad
content:
Tata Consultancy Services said its HyperVault unit and partners have committed 700 billion rupees, about $7.4B, to an AI data centre campus of up to one gigawatt in Hyderabad, using green energy and water-neutral design principles. EU rules require any data centre above 500kW to report total and drinking water consumption to a European database every year.
Tata Consultancy Services said its HyperVault unit and partners have committed 700 billion rupees, about $7.4B, to an AI data centre campus in southern India. Bloomberg News reported the exchange filing on Saturday.
The site sits on 264 acres in Hyderabad, in Telangana, and will have a capacity of up to one gigawatt. The land is already secured, and TCS expects the campus to rank among the largest AI infrastructure sites in India.
“The campus will support frontier AI companies and hyperscalers with high-density, liquid-cooled compute infrastructure on a global scale,” the company said.
TCS also says the project will use green energy and water-neutral design principles. Neither term is defined in the filing.
The money follows a pattern. TPG put $1B into the company’s data centre business last November, part of a wider flow of foreign capital into Indian AI infrastructure through local firms.
Two of those words carry obligations in Europe that they do not carry in India, and the gap is not rhetorical.
Any data centre in the EU with at least 500kW of installed IT power must report annually to a European database, under a delegated regulation adopted in 2024.
The indicators include total water consumption and drinking water consumption, from which water usage effectiveness is calculated. Energy demand, waste heat recovery and the renewable share are in there too.
The annual deadline is 15 May. The regulation itself sets out no penalty for not filing, so the discipline is disclosure rather than enforcement.
So water-neutral design is a phrase in Hyderabad and a filed number in Frankfurt. Neither guarantees the water, but only one leaves evidence.
The scale runs the other way. Europe has opened bidding for up to seven AI gigafactories worth roughly EUR 30B, of which about EUR 10B would be public money and only around EUR 1B of Brussels’ share is committed.
Construction there is targeted for early 2027. TCS is putting $7.4B into one campus now, most of it private money rather than public.
Europe built the measuring regime first and the gigawatts second. Its own gigafactory plan has already stumbled on delays, and this filing is what the other order looks like.

report.summary: TCS commits $7.4B to build a one-gigawatt AI data centre campus in Hyderabad, highlighting India's private-led infrastructure push versus Europe's disclosure-focused approach.
report.background: TCS HyperVault and partners have pledged 700 billion rupees ($7.4B) to develop an AI data centre campus on 264 acres in Hyderabad, India, with capacity up to one gigawatt. The project targets frontier AI companies and hyperscalers with high-density, liquid-cooled compute infrastructure, and TCS expects it to be among India's largest AI facilities. The investment follows TPG's $1B injection into TCS's data centre business in November, part of growing foreign interest in Indian AI infrastructure. The filing claims the campus will use green energy and water-neutral design principles, but neither is defined. In the EU, by contrast, any data centre above 500kW must annually report water and energy consumption to a European database under a 2024 delegated regulation. Europe's own AI gigafactory programme has faced delays, while TCS is building large-scale capacity now with mostly private money.
key_points: TCS HyperVault and partners have pledged $7.4B for a one-gigawatt AI data centre campus on 264 acres in Hyderabad, making it one of India's largest AI infrastructure projects. The investment is mostly private capital, unlike Europe's publicly supported AI gigafactory programme, and follows TPG's earlier $1B injection into TCS's data centre business.

The campus targets frontier AI companies and hyperscalers, providing high-density, liquid-cooled compute infrastructure at global scale. AI training workloads generate intense heat and require dense server configurations, so purpose-built liquid cooling is becoming essential. Older data centres often lack the power and cooling capacity for next-generation AI chips, making new projects like this strategically important.

TCS claims the campus will use green energy and water-neutral design, but the filing does not define either term. In the EU, data centres above 500kW must report annual energy use, renewable share, total water consumption and drinking water consumption to a central database by 15 May. Although the regulation sets no penalty, it leaves auditable evidence rather than just marketing language.

Europe has launched bidding for up to seven AI 'gigafactories' worth around €30B, with roughly €10B in public funds, but construction is targeted for 2027 and the plan has already faced delays. TCS is spending $7.4B on one campus now. This shows two approaches: India building capacity first with private money, Europe building a measurement and reporting framework first.
report.impact: This investment could significantly expand global AI compute supply outside the US and Europe, helping Indian developers and enterprises access powerful infrastructure closer to home, potentially reducing latency and dependence on foreign clouds. It also signals that private capital sees India as an AI infrastructure hub, which may attract further investment and talent. For regular users, faster and more affordable AI services could follow, although India still grapples with grid reliability and water stress. For the AI industry, the project demonstrates growing demand for purpose-built liquid-cooled data centres, while also raising accountability questions: without clear definitions of 'green energy' and 'water-neutral', sustainability claims remain hard to verify, unlike in Europe where reporting rules force disclosure.
report.tools: If you want to monitor similar moves, watch the EU Data Centre Database and the IEA's data centre energy reports. For practical standards, follow the Open Compute Project's liquid cooling and open rack specs, plus the Green Software Foundation's carbon-aware SDK for measuring software emissions. Tools like Cloud Carbon Footprint can help estimate data-centre energy and carbon footprints, while water footprint assessment methods based on ISO 14046 can be used to verify water-neutral claims.
